findings.failureScenario: keyword.export writes the keyword list with std::fs::write to any caller-supplied `path` (UI, CLI or MCP agent) and never calls Session::check_write_target. The app's stated invariant (originals.rs:1-5) is that files Ember writes for the user never land on a catalogued photo's original or XMP sidecar. Other writers enforce it (image exports via OriginalGuard, export.contactSheet, merge). `keyword.export {path: "/Photos/IMG_0001.xmp"}`, or the original raw path, silently truncates and replaces that file with a text keyword list. That destroys the photo's sidecar edits and metadata, or the original itself.
findings.action: Call `s.check_write_target(path)` before writing (as export.contactSheet does) and write atomically.

findings.failureScenario: metadata.downloadPlaceNames accepts an undocumented `base` parameter that may be any https:// host (base_allowed only checks the scheme). The fetched files carry no size or SHA-256 pin (`size: None, sha256: None`). They are then written as the gazetteer into `dataset`, which is also a caller-chosen folder. An agent or script driving the command interface can make the app fetch from an arbitrary host and install unverified place data. Reverse geocoding then writes that data into photo metadata (City/State/Country) across the library. This contrasts with the face-model downloader, which pins address, size and hash.
findings.action: Drop the `base` parameter from release builds (keep it behind cfg(test)/debug for the loopback test server) or pin the GeoNames files by size/hash.

So the app fetches from addresses that are neither built in nor pinned. Integrity still holds via the catalog's required sha256/size, but the documented trust boundary that reviewers and agents rely on is false.
findings.action: Correct the invariant to say catalog.json entries are user-supplied addresses verified by their declared hash/size (or restrict them to https).
